newsitem.title: GERMANY: Parliament starts passing Buba law but changes due.
newsitem.headline: Parliament starts passing Buba law but changes due.

text.p: Germany's upper house of parliament on Friday approved changes in the Bundesbank law to prepare it for Europe's monetary union (EMU), but the draft may have to be changed again to keep pace with Bonn's changing budget plans.

The upper house, which first handled the bill because it came from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet, approved the draft to transfer power for monetary policy from the Bundesbank to the European central bank due to take charge in 1999.

The new law would also bring German monetary authorities into line with others in the European Union and strengthen the Bundesbank's legendary independence by barring Bonn cabinet ministers from requesting delays in sensitive decisions.
But the law as it now stands will probably have to be changed to allow the Bundesbank to revalue its gold and currency reserves to provide Bonn with much-needed funds to help it qualify for EMU.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel announced on Thursday he wanted to use revalued Bundesbank gold to fill gaping holes in his 1997 budget caused by a massive 18 billion mark ($10.6 billion) shortfall in expected tax revenues this year.
A ministry spokeswoman said on Friday the gold could help Waigel's 1997 budget if the Bundesbank revalued it in an interim account this year.
Government officials in Bonn said the Bundesbank council seemed to see no problems with revaluing the reserves next year but some council members had doubts about doing it now.
The planned changes in the Bundesbank law were necessary to anchor the central bank in its future role as part of the European System of Central Banks (ESCB).
